claim: The study analyzed mtDNA from 1675 tumors across 31 tumor types.
source: In this study, we analyzed somatic alterations in mtDNA from 1675 tumors.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract and supported by Table 1 showing the breakdown of samples.

claim: 1907 somatic substitutions were identified in the study.
source: We identified 1907 somatic substitutions, which exhibited dramatic replicative strand bias, predominantly C > T and A > G on the mitochondrial heavy strand.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by the catalog of mutations.

claim: Somatic mtDNA substitutions exhibited dramatic replicative strand bias, predominantly C > T and A > G on the mitochondrial heavy strand.
source: We identified 1907 somatic substitutions, which exhibited dramatic replicative strand bias, predominantly C > T and A > G on the mitochondrial heavy strand.
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated through mutational signature analysis in Results.

claim: The strand-asymmetric signature of mtDNA mutations differs from those found in nuclear cancer genomes.
source: This strand-asymmetric mutational signature is not similar to any of the 21 cancer-associated mutational signatures recently identified from the nuclear DNA of 30 different cancer types (Alexandrov et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison with published nuclear genome signatures from Alexandrov et al., 2013.

claim: The mtDNA mutational signature matches the inferred germline process shaping primate mtDNA sequence content.
source: This strand-asymmetric signature differs from those found in nuclear cancer genomes but matches the inferred germline process shaping primate mtDNA sequence content.
evidence: Demonstrated through codon usage analysis and evolutionary simulations in the Results section.

claim: Missense mutations were selectively neutral.
source: Missense mutations were selectively neutral and often gradually drifted towards homoplasmy over time.
evidence: Supported by dN/dS ratio analysis showing value close to 1.

claim: Missense mutations often gradually drifted towards homoplasmy over time.
source: Missense mutations were selectively neutral and often gradually drifted towards homoplasmy over time.
evidence: Inferred from variant allele fraction distributions and paired sample analyses.

claim: Mutations resulting in protein truncation undergo negative selection.
source: In contrast, mutations resulting in protein truncation undergo negative selection and were almost exclusively heteroplasmic.
evidence: Demonstrated by significantly lower VAFs for nonsense mutations compared to missense mutations.

claim: Protein-truncating mutations were almost exclusively heteroplasmic.
source: In contrast, mutations resulting in protein truncation undergo negative selection and were almost exclusively heteroplasmic.
evidence: Shown by VAF analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: The endogenous mutational mechanism has far greater impact than any other external mutagens in mitochondria.
source: Our findings indicate that the endogenous mutational mechanism has far greater impact than any other external mutagens in mitochondria and is fundamentally linked to mtDNA replication.
evidence: Supported by lack of UV or tobacco signatures in melanoma and lung cancer mtDNA.

claim: The mtDNA mutational mechanism is fundamentally linked to mtDNA replication.
source: Our findings indicate that the endogenous mutational mechanism has far greater impact than any other external mutagens in mitochondria and is fundamentally linked to mtDNA replication.
evidence: Demonstrated by strand bias analysis and reversal of signature in D-loop region.

claim: Human cells have hundreds to thousands of mitochondria present in every cell.
source: Beyond the ∼3200 Mb of nuclear genomic DNA, human cells have hundreds to thousands of mitochondria present in every cell, each carrying one or a few copies of the 16,569 bp circular mitochondrial genomes (Smeitink et al., 2001; Legros et al., 2004; Koppenol et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from established literature (Smeitink et al., 2001; Legros et al., 2004; Koppenol et al., 2011).

claim: Each mitochondrion carries one or a few copies of the 16,569 bp circular mitochondrial genome.
source: Beyond the ∼3200 Mb of nuclear genomic DNA, human cells have hundreds to thousands of mitochondria present in every cell, each carrying one or a few copies of the 16,569 bp circular mitochondrial genomes (Smeitink et al., 2001; Legros et al., 2004; Koppenol et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from established literature (Smeitink et al., 2001; Legros et al., 2004; Koppenol et al., 2011).

claim: Mitochondria are involved in cellular energy balance through oxidative phosphorylation.
source: In addition to their role in cellular energy balance through oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondria are involved in many essential cellular functions including modulation of oxidation–reduction status, contribution to cytosolic biosynthetic precursors, and initiation of apoptosis.
evidence: General knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondria are involved in modulation of oxidation-reduction status.
source: In addition to their role in cellular energy balance through oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondria are involved in many essential cellular functions including modulation of oxidation–reduction status, contribution to cytosolic biosynthetic precursors, and initiation of apoptosis.
evidence: General knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondria contribute to cytosolic biosynthetic precursors.
source: In addition to their role in cellular energy balance through oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondria are involved in many essential cellular functions including modulation of oxidation–reduction status, contribution to cytosolic biosynthetic precursors, and initiation of apoptosis.
evidence: General knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondria initiate apoptosis.
source: In addition to their role in cellular energy balance through oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondria are involved in many essential cellular functions including modulation of oxidation–reduction status, contribution to cytosolic biosynthetic precursors, and initiation of apoptosis.
evidence: General knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondria in eukaryotic cells evolved by endosymbiosis from a free-living α-proteobacterium.
source: Mitochondria in eukaryotic cells evolved by endosymbiosis from a free-living α-proteobacterium (Gray et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited from Gray et al., 1999.

claim: Over 2 billion years of co-evolution, many ancestral mitochondrial genes have transferred to the nucleus.
source: Over 2 billion years of co-evolution, many ancestral mitochondrial genes have transferred to the nucleus (Falkenberg et al., 2007; Calvo and Mootha, 2010; Wallace, 2012).
evidence: Cited from Falkenberg et al., 2007; Calvo and Mootha, 2010; Wallace, 2012.

claim: The heavy (H) strand of mtDNA is guanine-rich with C/G ratio of 0.4.
source: The heavy (H) strand is guanine-rich (C/G = 0.4) and is the template from which most mitochondrial proteins (12 out of 13) are transcribed, whereas only one protein-coding gene, MT-ND6, is transcribed from the correspondingly cytosine-rich light (L) strand.
evidence: Stated as a known characteristic of mtDNA.

claim: 12 out of 13 mitochondrial proteins are transcribed from the heavy strand.
source: The heavy (H) strand is guanine-rich (C/G = 0.4) and is the template from which most mitochondrial proteins (12 out of 13) are transcribed, whereas only one protein-coding gene, MT-ND6, is transcribed from the correspondingly cytosine-rich light (L) strand.
evidence: Stated as a known characteristic of mtDNA.

claim: Only one protein-coding gene, MT-ND6, is transcribed from the light strand.
source: The heavy (H) strand is guanine-rich (C/G = 0.4) and is the template from which most mitochondrial proteins (12 out of 13) are transcribed, whereas only one protein-coding gene, MT-ND6, is transcribed from the correspondingly cytosine-rich light (L) strand.
evidence: Stated as a known characteristic of mtDNA.

claim: Mutations in the mitochondrial genome cause inherited disease.
source: Mutations in the mitochondrial genome cause inherited disease (Chinnery, 1993), with a maternal inheritance pattern because only eggs contribute mitochondria to the zygote.
evidence: Cited from Chinnery, 1993.

claim: Mitochondrial disease has a maternal inheritance pattern because only eggs contribute mitochondria to the zygote.
source: Mutations in the mitochondrial genome cause inherited disease (Chinnery, 1993), with a maternal inheritance pattern because only eggs contribute mitochondria to the zygote.
evidence: General knowledge about mitochondrial inheritance.

claim: Cancer-specific mtDNA mutations have been previously reported.
source: Although cancer-specific mutations have been previously reported (Polyak et al., 1998; Brandon et al., 2006; Chatterjee et al., 2006; He et al., 2010; Larman et al., 2012), the limited sample size or poor sensitivity of capillary sequencing for heteroplasmic mutations has not allowed a comprehensive analysis of the mutational signatures of mitochondrial mutations nor their likely functional significance.
evidence: Cited from multiple studies (Polyak et al., 1998; Brandon et al., 2006; Chatterjee et al., 2006; He et al., 2010; Larman et al., 2012).

claim: Previous studies had limited sample size or poor sensitivity of capillary sequencing for heteroplasmic mutations.
source: Although cancer-specific mutations have been previously reported (Polyak et al., 1998; Brandon et al., 2006; Chatterjee et al., 2006; He et al., 2010; Larman et al., 2012), the limited sample size or poor sensitivity of capillary sequencing for heteroplasmic mutations has not allowed a comprehensive analysis of the mutational signatures of mitochondrial mutations nor their likely functional significance.
evidence: Assessment of previous literature limitations.

claim: Previous reports suggested that mitochondrial somatic mutations might be under positive selection.
source: Previous reports suggested that mitochondrial somatic mutations might be under positive selection and thus contribute to cancer development, but the small number of reported mutations renders this conclusion uncertain (Brandon et al., 2006; Chatterjee et al., 2006; Larman et al., 2012; Schon et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from Brandon et al., 2006; Chatterjee et al., 2006; Larman et al., 2012; Schon et al., 2012.

claim: Cancer cells have greatly increased energy demands over normal cells.
source: Nonetheless, the hypothesis of functionally relevant mitochondrial mutations is an appealing one because cancer cells have greatly increased energy demands over normal cells and demonstrate a switch from aerobic glycolysis in mitochondria to lactic acid fermentation in the cytosol (the Warburg effect) (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Koppenol et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Koppenol et al., 2011.

claim: Cancer cells demonstrate a switch from aerobic glycolysis in mitochondria to lactic acid fermentation in the cytosol (the Warburg effect).
source: Nonetheless, the hypothesis of functionally relevant mitochondrial mutations is an appealing one because cancer cells have greatly increased energy demands over normal cells and demonstrate a switch from aerobic glycolysis in mitochondria to lactic acid fermentation in the cytosol (the Warburg effect) (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Koppenol et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Koppenol et al., 2011.

claim: More than 20 mutational signatures operative in cancers have been identified in the nuclear genome.
source: Recently, >20 mutational signatures operative in cancers have been identified in the nuclear genome (Alexandrov et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Alexandrov et al., 2013.

claim: The study extracted mtDNA sequences from 704 whole-genome and 971 whole-exome sequencing data.
source: We extracted the mtDNA sequences from 704 whole-genome and 971 whole-exome sequencing data generated on primary cancers and compared them with mtDNA sequences from their matched normal samples.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the methodology.

claim: Standard coverage of 30-40× in the nuclear genome provides significantly greater coverage of the mitochondrial genome (average read depth = 7901.0×).
source: Given the abundance of mtDNA per cancer cell, a standard coverage of 30–40× in the nuclear genome provides significantly greater coverage of the mitochondrial genome (average read depth = 7901.0×), enabling accurate identification of somatic mutations including rare heteroplasmic variants.
evidence: Calculated from sequencing data.

claim: Whole-exome sequencing provided an average read depth of 92.1× across the mitochondrial genome.
source: We found an average read depth of 92.1× across the mitochondrial genome in exome studies.
evidence: Calculated from sequencing data.

claim: The overall read depths between whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing correlated strongly (R2 = 0.59).
source: From 139 samples in which we had both exome and whole-genome sequencing data, the overall read depths correlated strongly (R2 = 0.59, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) as did variant allele fractions for mtDNA somatic mutations (R2 = 0.97, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Variant allele fractions for mtDNA somatic mutations correlated strongly between whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing (R2 = 0.97).
source: From 139 samples in which we had both exome and whole-genome sequencing data, the overall read depths correlated strongly (R2 = 0.59, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) as did variant allele fractions for mtDNA somatic mutations (R2 = 0.97, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The sensitivity of whole-exome sequencing for detection of mtDNA somatic mutations was 71.4% compared to whole-genome sequencing.
source: Validation experiments suggested the sensitivity of whole-exome sequencing for detection of mtDNA somatic mutations to be 71.4% compared to whole-genome sequencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and 'Materials and Methods', 'Off-target mtDNA reads in whole-exome sequencing' and 'DNA cross-contamination').
evidence: Determined through validation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Variants were only reported with an allele fraction of >3%.
source: To reduce potential false-positive calls of mtDNA somatic mutations, we only report variants called with an allele fraction of >3%.
evidence: Stated as a methodological criterion.

claim: mtDNA copy numbers are 100-1000 times higher than nuclear genomes in human somatic cells.
source: This eliminates the risk of miscalls due to mtDNA-derived pseudogenes in the nucleus (NuMTs) because mtDNA copy numbers are 100–1000 times higher than nuclear genomes in human somatic cells, and the sequence homology between mtDNA and NuMTs presented in the human reference genome is generally <95% (in 96 out of 101 NuMTs with length greater than 300 bp).
evidence: General knowledge about mtDNA copy number.

claim: The sequence homology between mtDNA and NuMTs in the human reference genome is generally <95% (in 96 out of 101 NuMTs with length greater than 300 bp).
source: This eliminates the risk of miscalls due to mtDNA-derived pseudogenes in the nucleus (NuMTs) because mtDNA copy numbers are 100–1000 times higher than nuclear genomes in human somatic cells, and the sequence homology between mtDNA and NuMTs presented in the human reference genome is generally <95% (in 96 out of 101 NuMTs with length greater than 300 bp).
evidence: Analysis of reference genome data.

claim: 976 (58.3%) of the 1675 cancer samples harbored at least one somatic substitution.
source: Of the 1675 cancer samples, 976 (58.3%) harbored at least one somatic substitution and 521 (31.1%) had multiple substitutions, ranging from 2 to 7 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Calculated from the data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 521 (31.1%) cancer samples had multiple substitutions, ranging from 2 to 7.
source: Of the 1675 cancer samples, 976 (58.3%) harbored at least one somatic substitution and 521 (31.1%) had multiple substitutions, ranging from 2 to 7 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Calculated from the data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Of 1209 (63.4%) somatic substitutions, these were not registered in the databases of mtDNA common polymorphism.
source: Of these 1907 somatic substitutions, 1209 (63.4%) were not registered in the databases of mtDNA common polymorphism (Ingman and Gyllensten, 2006; Levin et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison with mtDB database (Ingman and Gyllensten, 2006; Levin et al., 2013).

claim: When examining substitutions found in both tumor and normal samples, only 21 (0.05%) were not registered in polymorphism databases.
source: In comparison, when we examined substitutions found in both the tumor and the normal samples from a patient, only 21 (0.05%) were not registered in the polymorphism databases, a significantly different fraction from the tumor-only variants (p < 10−10; Chi-squared test).
evidence: Comparison with polymorphism databases.

claim: 595 (31.2%) recurrent mutations were found that can be collapsed onto 246 mtDNA positions.
source: We found 595 (31.2%) recurrent mutations that can be collapsed onto 246 mtDNA positions, which is a 6.9-fold higher level of recurrence than expected by chance (p < 10−10).
evidence: Calculated from mutation data.

claim: The level of recurrence is 6.9-fold higher than expected by chance (p < 10−10).
source: We found 595 (31.2%) recurrent mutations that can be collapsed onto 246 mtDNA positions, which is a 6.9-fold higher level of recurrence than expected by chance (p < 10−10).
evidence: Statistical analysis of mutation recurrence.

claim: The generation or fixation of mtDNA mutations is not random, but influenced by factors such as the underlying mutational process or positive selection.
source: This suggests that the generation or fixation of mtDNA mutations is not random, but influenced by factors such as the underlying mutational process or positive selection.
evidence: Inferred from the high level of recurrence.

claim: 72 pairs of mutations were sufficiently close to phase.
source: In those with multiple substitutions, 72 pairs of mutations were sufficiently close to phase (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012b) such that we could determine whether they were linked on the same mtDNA genome or were on different copies.
evidence: Analysis of mutation phasing from sequencing data.

claim: 45 (62.5%) pairs of mutations were linked on the same mtDNA genome.
source: We found that 45 (62.5%) pairs of mutations were linked on the same mtDNA genome (Supplementary file 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Supplementary file 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Of the linked mutations, 33 showed a clear temporal order where one mutation was demonstrably sub-clonal to the other.
source: Furthermore, of these linked mutations, 33 showed a clear temporal order: that is, one mutation was demonstrably sub-clonal to the other.
evidence: Analysis of variant allele fractions for phased mutations.

claim: The number of somatic mtDNA substitutions varied significantly according to tumor type (p = 4.4 × 10−52).
source: The number of somatic mtDNA substitutions varied significantly according to tumor type (p = 4.4 × 10−52) after correcting for confounding variables such as sequencing coverage: gastric, hepatocellular, prostate, and colorectal cancers had the highest number of mtDNA substitutions (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gastric, hepatocellular, prostate, and colorectal cancers had the highest number of mtDNA substitutions.
source: The number of somatic mtDNA substitutions varied significantly according to tumor type (p = 4.4 × 10−52) after correcting for confounding variables such as sequencing coverage: gastric, hepatocellular, prostate, and colorectal cancers had the highest number of mtDNA substitutions (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hematologic cancers (acute lymphoblastic leukemia, myeloproliferative disease, and myelodysplastic syndrome) had fewer mutations.
source: In contrast, hematologic cancers (acute lymphoblastic leukemia, myeloproliferative disease, and myelodysplastic syndrome) had fewer mutations.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the number of mtDNA somatic mutations and age at diagnosis in breast cancers (p = 0.0004).
source: Interestingly, we find a positive correlation between the number of mtDNA somatic mutations and age at diagnosis in breast cancers (p = 0.0004; Figure 2C), in keeping with the idea that the number of mitochondrial generations is linked to mutation burden.
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: C > T and T > C transitions constituted 90.9% of all the 1907 substitutions.
source: With respect to signatures of somatic substitutions, C > T and T > C transitions constituted 90.9% of all the 1907 substitutions (Figure 1) among the six classes of possible base substitutions.
evidence: Calculated from mutation data shown in Figure 1.

claim: 84.1% of the C > T transitions were on the H strand.
source: 84.1% of the C > T transitions were on the H strand.
evidence: Calculated from mutation data.

claim: The C > T substitution rate is 12.6-fold higher on the H strand than the L strand.
source: This level of strand bias occurred despite the fact that cytosine is 2.4-fold less common on the H than the L strand, so the C > T substitution rate is 12.6-fold higher on the H strand.
evidence: Calculated from mutation data accounting for nucleotide composition.

claim: 76.8% of the T > C transitions were on the L strand.
source: By contrast, 76.8% of the T > C transitions were on the L strand despite its lower thymine content (1.3-fold less than the H strand).
evidence: Calculated from mutation data.

claim: The T > C mutation rate on the L strand is 4.2-fold higher than on the H strand.
source: This implies that the T > C mutation rate on the L strand is 4.2-fold higher than on the H strand.
evidence: Calculated from mutation data accounting for nucleotide composition.

claim: CH > TH substitutions were enriched for the NpCpG trinucleotide context (8- to 15-fold more frequent than expected by chance).
source: CH > TH substitutions (i.e. C > T mutations on the H strand) were enriched for the NpCpG trinucleotide context (8- to 15-fold more frequent than expected by chance; Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TL > CL substitutions showed 5- to 8-fold enrichment in NpTpC.
source: By contrast, TL > CL substitutions (i.e. T > C mutations on the L strand) showed 5- to 8-fold enrichment in NpTpC.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The mutational signatures were broadly consistent across tumor types.
source: Of the 18 tumor types that presented at least 25 mtDNA somatic substitutions in this study, the mutational signatures were broadly consistent across tumor types (Figure 3B), with the exception that multiple myeloma had a somewhat higher rate of TH > CH changes than other histologies (p = 8.1 × 10−6).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Multiple myeloma had a somewhat higher rate of TH > CH changes than other histologies (p = 8.1 × 10−6).
source: Of the 18 tumor types that presented at least 25 mtDNA somatic substitutions in this study, the mutational signatures were broadly consistent across tumor types (Figure 3B), with the exception that multiple myeloma had a somewhat higher rate of TH > CH changes than other histologies (p = 8.1 × 10−6).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The strand bias always favors CH > TH and TL > CL whether the gene is transcribed from the H strand or from the L strand.
source: However, we find that the strand bias always favors CH > TH and TL > CL whether the gene is transcribed from the H strand or from the L strand (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mtDNA mutational strand bias is not compatible with transcription-coupled repair.
source: This is not compatible with transcription-coupled repair, for which the direction of strand bias is fundamentally dictated by which strand is transcribed.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that strand bias is independent of transcription direction.

claim: The mtDNA mutational strand bias appears to be driven by differences in replication between the two strands.
source: Instead, the mtDNA mutational strand bias reported here appears to be driven by differences in replication between the two strands.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of strand bias and its reversal in the D-loop.

claim: mtDNA replication initiates from an origin of replication (OH) in the D-loop, with the nascent H and the L strand replicating as leading and lagging strand, respectively.
source: mtDNA replication harbors substantial strand asymmetry between the H and L strands: mtDNA replication initiates from an origin of replication (OH) in the D-loop, with the nascent H and the L strand replicating as leading and lagging strand, respectively (Clayton, 1982; Falkenberg et al., 2007; Holt and Reyes, 2012).
evidence: Cited from Clayton, 1982; Falkenberg et al., 2007; Holt and Reyes, 2012.

claim: C > T substitutions were prevalent in the leading (heavy) strand.
source: We observed that C > T substitutions were prevalent in the leading (heavy) strand, whereas T > C substitutions were found in the lagging (light) strand (Figure 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1.

claim: T > C substitutions were found in the lagging (light) strand.
source: We observed that C > T substitutions were prevalent in the leading (heavy) strand, whereas T > C substitutions were found in the lagging (light) strand (Figure 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1.

claim: The strand bias was reversed in the D-loop itself.
source: Remarkably, this strand bias was reversed in the D-loop itself (Figures 1 and 3C), further suggesting that the mtDNA somatic mutations are replication-coupled: according to a recently proposed bidirectional model of mtDNA replication (Yasukawa et al., 2005, 2006; Holt and Reyes, 2012), mtDNA replication is also able to initiate from the so-called Ori-b site, typically located around genomic position 16,197 and proceeds on both strands away from the origin (Figure 1).
evidence: Shown in Figures 1 and 3C.

claim: According to the bidirectional model, mtDNA replication can initiate from the Ori-b site, typically located around genomic position 16,197.
source: Remarkably, this strand bias was reversed in the D-loop itself (Figures 1 and 3C), further suggesting that the mtDNA somatic mutations are replication-coupled: according to a recently proposed bidirectional model of mtDNA replication (Yasukawa et al., 2005, 2006; Holt and Reyes, 2012), mtDNA replication is also able to initiate from the so-called Ori-b site, typically located around genomic position 16,197 and proceeds on both strands away from the origin (Figure 1).
evidence: Cited from Yasukawa et al., 2005, 2006; Holt and Reyes, 2012.

claim: The mutational mechanism which has generated the CH > TH and TL > CL signature in cancer mtDNA is equivalent to the one that has been operating during evolution of human germline mtDNA.
source: It appears that the mutational mechanism which has generated the CH > TH and TL > CL signature in cancer mtDNA is equivalent to the one that has been operating during evolution of human germline mtDNA (Nikolaou and Almirantis, 2006).
evidence: Inferred from codon usage analysis and cited from Nikolaou and Almirantis, 2006.

claim: The GCG triplet codon (Alanine) is 15.8-fold less frequently observed in the 12 mtDNA protein-coding genes that are transcribed from the H strand compared to its synonymous GCA codon.
source: For example, the GCG triplet codon (Alanine) appears to have been replaced by its synonymous GCA codon (due to CH > TH (GL > AL)), with the former being 15.8-fold less frequently observed in the 12 mtDNA protein-coding genes that are transcribed from the H strand (and encoded on the L strand).
evidence: Analysis of codon usage in mtDNA.

claim: All 32 synonymous codon pairs present the same tendency of codon depletion.
source: All 32 synonymous codon pairs present the same tendency.
evidence: Analysis of codon usage shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The gene transcribed from the L strand (MT-ND6) demonstrates the opposite direction of codon skew.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the gene transcribed from the L strand (MT-ND6) demonstrates the opposite direction of skew.
evidence: Analysis of codon usage.

claim: The CH > TH and TL > CL mutational pressure may be characteristic of vertebrates, and primates in particular.
source: Further analyses of mtDNA codon usage from seven animal species suggest that the CH > TH and TL > CL mutational pressure may be characteristic of vertebrates, and primates in particular (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The actual sequence composition of the human mitochondrial genome strongly resembles the stationary distribution from evolutionary simulations (Pearson's r = 0.83; p < 0.0001).
source: The actual sequence composition of the human mitochondrial genome strongly resembles this stationary distribution (Pearson's r = 0.83; p < 0.0001; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Simulations with a random sequence encoding the exact amino acid sequence of the reference mitochondrial genome eventually approximate the observed human mitochondrial genome (Pearson's r = 0.96, p < 0.0001).
source: In a second simulation, a random sequence encoding the exact amino acid sequence of the reference mitochondrial genome was evolved by synonymous mutations under the observed mtDNA signature until reaching a stationary sequence composition (mutation–selection equilibrium). These simulations also eventually approximate the observed human mitochondrial genome (Pearson's r = 0.96, p < 0.0001; Figure 4B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mitochondrial mutation signature observed in cancer cells closely reflects the mutation signature active in the germline.
source: These analyses strongly suggest that the mitochondrial mutation signature observed in cancer cells closely reflects the mutation signature active in the germline, which has continuously shaped the mitochondrial genome during human evolution.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary simulations and codon usage analysis.

claim: Of the 1907 substitutions, 1153 (60.5%) were in the 13 protein-coding genes.
source: Of the 1907 substitutions, 1153 (60.5%) were in the 13 protein-coding genes.
evidence: Calculated from mutation data.

claim: The 1153 substitutions in protein-coding genes include 63 nonsense, 4 stop-lost, 878 missense, and 208 silent substitutions.
source: These include 63 nonsense, 4 stop-lost, 878 missense, and 208 silent substitutions (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Calculated from mutation data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Out of 251 indels observed, 110 occurred within protein-coding genes.
source: In addition, out of 251 indels we observed, 110 occurred within protein-coding genes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Calculated from mutation data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 245 (27.9%) of the missense substitutions were recurrent, affecting 107 distinct mtDNA sites.
source: Of the missense substitutions, 245 (27.9%) were recurrent, affecting 107 distinct mtDNA sites.
evidence: Calculated from mutation data.

claim: Silent substitutions were also frequently recurrent (28 recurrent variants in 13 mtDNA sites).
source: Although this very high level of mutation clustering could, at first sight, be interpreted as evidence for positive selection, we found that silent substitutions were also frequently recurrent (28 recurrent variants in 13 mtDNA sites), with no substantial difference in recurrence rates between silent and missense mutations (p = 0.19; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Calculated from mutation data and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no substantial difference in recurrence rates between silent and missense mutations (p = 0.19).
source: Although this very high level of mutation clustering could, at first sight, be interpreted as evidence for positive selection, we found that silent substitutions were also frequently recurrent (28 recurrent variants in 13 mtDNA sites), with no substantial difference in recurrence rates between silent and missense mutations (p = 0.19; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ratio of somatic missense to silent substitutions (Rms:s) is 4.2 (878/208).
source: The ratio of somatic missense to silent substitutions (Rms:s) is apparently higher (4.2, 878/208) than that observed for cancer-associated somatic mutations in nuclear DNA (generally around 2:1 to 3:1 across tumor types) (Greenman et al., 2007; Nik-Zainal et al., 2012a).
evidence: Calculated from mutation data and compared to nuclear DNA ratios from Greenman et al., 2007; Nik-Zainal et al., 2012a.

claim: The dN/dS ratio for missense mutations is 1.21 (95% confidence interval, 1.015–1.434; p = 0.031).
source: In keeping with this, a dN/dS ratio (See 'Materials and Methods') calculated taking into account both the mutational signature and the mtDNA codon usage revealed that missense mutations accumulate at a frequency very close to that expected under neutrality (dN/dS = 1.21; 95% confidence interval, 1.015–1.434; p = 0.031).
evidence: Statistical analysis using dN/dS method.

claim: The vast majority of mtDNA mutations are passengers with no convincing evidence suggesting the existence of driver mitochondrial DNA mutations.
source: This indicates that despite the apparent high ratio of missense to silent mutations, the vast majority of mtDNA mutations are passengers with no convincing evidence suggesting the existence of driver mitochondrial DNA mutations.
evidence: Inferred from dN/dS analysis showing neutrality.

claim: No single gene had a higher than expected rate of missense or nonsense mutations.
source: Additional gene-by-gene analysis further revealed that no single gene had a higher than expected rate of missense or nonsense mutations (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Gene-by-gene analysis in Supplementary file 4.

claim: The overall ratio of nonsense mutations to silent mutations is exactly that expected by chance (dNonsense/dS = 1.004; 95% confidence interval, 0.699–1.443; p = 0.98).
source: Taking into account the mutation signature and amino acid composition of the mitochondrial genome, the overall ratio of nonsense mutations to silent mutations is exactly that expected by chance (dNonsense/dS = 1.004; 95% confidence interval, 0.699–1.443; p = 0.98).
evidence: Statistical analysis using dN/dS method.

claim: Missense and silent substitutions exhibited equivalent variant allele fractions (average VAFs; 40.1% and 40.9%, respectively; p = 0.8).
source: However, while missense and silent substitutions exhibited equivalent variant allele fractions (average VAFs; 40.1% and 40.9%, respectively; p = 0.8), nonsense substitutions presented significantly lower VAFs (average 26.4%; p = 6x10−5), as did frameshift indels (average 25.0%; p = 2 × 10−3; Figure 5A).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nonsense substitutions presented significantly lower VAFs (average 26.4%; p = 6x10−5).
source: However, while missense and silent substitutions exhibited equivalent variant allele fractions (average VAFs; 40.1% and 40.9%, respectively; p = 0.8), nonsense substitutions presented significantly lower VAFs (average 26.4%; p = 6x10−5), as did frameshift indels (average 25.0%; p = 2 × 10−3; Figure 5A).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Frameshift indels presented significantly lower VAFs (average 25.0%; p = 2 × 10−3).
source: However, while missense and silent substitutions exhibited equivalent variant allele fractions (average VAFs; 40.1% and 40.9%, respectively; p = 0.8), nonsense substitutions presented significantly lower VAFs (average 26.4%; p = 6x10−5), as did frameshift indels (average 25.0%; p = 2 × 10−3; Figure 5A).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nonsense mutations occur at the expected rate given the underlying mutational process.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that nonsense mutations occur at the expected rate given the underlying mutational process.
evidence: Inferred from dNonsense/dS ratio being close to 1.

claim: Cancer cells carrying deleterious mutations at or near homoplasmy are at a selective disadvantage.
source: The inference here is that cancer cells carrying such deleterious mutations at or near homoplasmy are at a selective disadvantage and hence do not contribute to clonal expansions, underlining the importance of functional mitochondria to cancer cells.
evidence: Inferred from lower VAFs of protein-truncating mutations.

claim: Colorectal cancers show less negative selection compared to breast cancers (p = 0.028).
source: The extent of such disadvantage may vary according to tumor type: for example colorectal cancers show less negative selection compared to breast cancers (p = 0.028; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: 171 mtDNA substitutions were found in mitochondrial tRNA sequences.
source: We found 171 mtDNA substitutions in mitochondrial tRNA sequences, which are very similar to the expected number (168.2, p = 0.82) from the mutational signature.
evidence: Calculated from mutation data.

claim: The number of tRNA substitutions (171) is very similar to the expected number (168.2, p = 0.82) from the mutational signature.
source: We found 171 mtDNA substitutions in mitochondrial tRNA sequences, which are very similar to the expected number (168.2, p = 0.82) from the mutational signature.
evidence: Statistical comparison with expected values.

claim: None of the substitutions was located in the trinucleotide anticodon site of the tRNA (expected number = 7.6, p = 0.006).
source: Interestingly, none of the substitutions was located in the trinucleotide anticodon site of the tRNA (expected number = 7.6, p = 0.006).
evidence: Statistical comparison with expected values.

claim: Mutations in tRNA anticodons confer a similar selective disadvantage as protein-truncating mutations.
source: This suggests that mutations in tRNA anticodons confer a similar selective disadvantage as protein-truncating mutations, presumably because such mutations would lead to systematic erroneous aminoacylation of nascent proteins during translation of the relevant codon.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of anticodon mutations.

claim: 16 (0.8%) of the 1907 somatic substitutions overlapped with known disease-associated mtDNA mutations.
source: Out of the 1907 somatic substitutions, 16 (0.8%) overlapped with known disease-associated mtDNA mutations, such as mutations frequently detected in MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes) and LHON (Leber hereditary optic neuropathy) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Comparison with known disease mutations in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Ten mutations within mitochondrial protein-coding, tRNA and rRNA genes showed significantly higher recurrent rate than expected from background mutational signature.
source: In addition, ten mutations within mitochondrial protein-coding, tRNA and rRNA genes showed significantly higher recurrent rate than expected from background mutational signature (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Statistical analysis in Supplementary file 5.

claim: 73 late (metastasis or relapse) cancer samples were sequenced in addition to the primary tissues.
source: As mentioned earlier, 73 late (metastasis or relapse) cancer samples were sequenced in addition to the primary tissues.
evidence: Stated in the Results section.

claim: Among the mtDNA mutations identified in paired cancer samples, there were mutations at high VAF in the primary not found in the metastasis (n = 49).
source: Among the mtDNA mutations identified in either of the paired cancer samples, a number of different patterns were observed. There were mutations at high VAF in the primary not found in the metastasis (n = 49); mutations in the metastasis not found in the primary (n = 49); and shared mutations (n = 71) at high or low VAF, sometimes with evidence for drift (VAF difference >0.2) between the two samples (n = 25).
evidence: Analysis of paired samples.

claim: There were mutations in the metastasis not found in the primary (n = 49).
source: Among the mtDNA mutations identified in either of the paired cancer samples, a number of different patterns were observed. There were mutations at high VAF in the primary not found in the metastasis (n = 49); mutations in the metastasis not found in the primary (n = 49); and shared mutations (n = 71) at high or low VAF, sometimes with evidence for drift (VAF difference >0.2) between the two samples (n = 25).
evidence: Analysis of paired samples.

claim: There were shared mutations (n = 71) at high or low VAF between primary and metastatic samples.
source: Among the mtDNA mutations identified in either of the paired cancer samples, a number of different patterns were observed. There were mutations at high VAF in the primary not found in the metastasis (n = 49); mutations in the metastasis not found in the primary (n = 49); and shared mutations (n = 71) at high or low VAF, sometimes with evidence for drift (VAF difference >0.2) between the two samples (n = 25).
evidence: Analysis of paired samples.

claim: 25 shared mutations showed evidence for drift (VAF difference >0.2) between primary and metastatic samples.
source: Among the mtDNA mutations identified in either of the paired cancer samples, a number of different patterns were observed. There were mutations at high VAF in the primary not found in the metastasis (n = 49); mutations in the metastasis not found in the primary (n = 49); and shared mutations (n = 71) at high or low VAF, sometimes with evidence for drift (VAF difference >0.2) between the two samples (n = 25).
evidence: Analysis of paired samples.

claim: Mitochondrial mutations can occur throughout the time course of tumor evolution.
source: These data, particularly the mutations found in the metastasis only, suggest that mitochondrial mutations can occur throughout the time course of tumor evolution, and still drift to homoplasmy with appreciable frequency, as suggested previously (Coller et al., 2001).
evidence: Inferred from paired sample analysis and cited from Coller et al., 2001.

claim: Based on a mutation rate of 10−7/base-pair/generation, there is on average ∼1 homoplasmic mutation for every 1000 cell generations.
source: Based on a mutation rate of 10−7/base-pair/generation (Coller et al., 2001; Hudson and Chinnery, 2006), this leads to an average ∼1 homoplasmic mutation for every 1000 cell generations.
evidence: Calculated from modeling and cited mutation rate from Coller et al., 2001; Hudson and Chinnery, 2006.

claim: In cancers associated with tobacco, there was no evidence of the mutational signatures characteristic of tobacco among the mtDNA mutations.
source: In cancers associated with exogenous mutagens, such as tobacco-associated lung cancer and ultraviolet light-associated melanomas, we found no evidence of the mutational signatures characteristic of these carcinogens among the mtDNA mutations (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: In cancers associated with ultraviolet light, there was no evidence of the mutational signatures characteristic of UV among the mtDNA mutations.
source: In cancers associated with exogenous mutagens, such as tobacco-associated lung cancer and ultraviolet light-associated melanomas, we found no evidence of the mutational signatures characteristic of these carcinogens among the mtDNA mutations (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations showed no evident influence on mitochondrial genomes in breast cancer.
source: Moreover, BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations showed no evident influence on mitochondrial genomes in breast cancer (Figure 5C), in contrast to their effects on nuclear genomes exhibiting an even distribution of mutations across all trinucleotide contexts (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012a; Alexandrov et al., 2013).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5C and compared to nuclear genome effects from Nik-Zainal et al., 2012a; Alexandrov et al., 2013.

claim: The primary mtDNA mutational process is endogenous to mitochondria and is very different to those operating in nuclear DNA.
source: Taken together, it appears that the primary mtDNA mutational process is endogenous to mitochondria and is very different to those operating in nuclear DNA.
evidence: Inferred from lack of exogenous mutagen signatures.

claim: The endogenous mutation rate is several orders of magnitude greater than that expected for exogenous carcinogens.
source: The simulations described above suggest the major explanation to be that the endogenous mutation rate is several orders of magnitude greater than that expected for exogenous carcinogens, thus swamping any signal.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary simulations and lack of exogenous signatures.

claim: The majority of the variants found are genuinely acquired somatically.
source: We believe the majority of the variants we find are genuinely acquired somatically.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of evidence including phasing analysis and comparison with polymorphism databases.

claim: Of the 45 pairs of somatic mutations phased together on the same copy of the mtDNA genome, at least 33 (73.3%) showed a clear sub-clonal relationship.
source: First, of the 45 pairs of somatic mutations phased together on the same copy of the mtDNA genome, at least 33 (73.3%) showed a clear sub-clonal relationship and therefore their occurrence is separated in time, or apparently somatic.
evidence: Analysis of phased mutations.

claim: Somatic substitutions are unlikely to be attributable to reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: On the basis of the mutational signature observed here, somatic substitutions are unlikely to be attributable to reactive oxygen species (ROS), as previous reports have suggested (Polyak et al., 1998; Larman et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from mutational signature analysis and cited from Polyak et al., 1998; Larman et al., 2012.

claim: Guanine oxidation by ROS predominantly causes G:C > T:A transversion.
source: Guanine oxidation by ROS predominantly causes G:C > T:A transversion (Thilly, 2003; Delaney et al., 2012), which constitute only 4.0% of the mutations in our data (Figure 5C).
evidence: Cited from Thilly, 2003; Delaney et al., 2012 and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: G:C > T:A transversions constitute only 4.0% of the mutations in the data.
source: Guanine oxidation by ROS predominantly causes G:C > T:A transversion (Thilly, 2003; Delaney et al., 2012), which constitute only 4.0% of the mutations in our data (Figure 5C).
evidence: Calculated from mutation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The parent H strand, displaced and single-stranded during mtDNA replication, could be more prone to cytosine deamination (generating CH > TH).
source: First, the parent H strand, displaced and single-stranded during mtDNA replication (Holt and Reyes, 2012), could be more prone to cytosine deamination (generating CH > TH) and/or adenine deamination (Lindahl, 1993; Saccone et al., 1999; Faith and Pollock, 2003) (generating TL > CL).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on known biochemistry cited from Holt and Reyes, 2012; Lindahl, 1993; Saccone et al., 1999; Faith and Pollock, 2003.

claim: The parent H strand could be more prone to adenine deamination (generating TL > CL).
source: First, the parent H strand, displaced and single-stranded during mtDNA replication (Holt and Reyes, 2012), could be more prone to cytosine deamination (generating CH > TH) and/or adenine deamination (Lindahl, 1993; Saccone et al., 1999; Faith and Pollock, 2003) (generating TL > CL).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on known biochemistry cited from Lindahl, 1993; Saccone et al., 1999; Faith and Pollock, 2003.

claim: Endogenous mtDNA polymerase (POLG) replication errors could be preferentially generated on the leading strand.
source: Secondly, endogenous mtDNA polymerase (POLG) replication errors (Zheng et al., 2006) (which show the pattern of C > T and A > G substitutions) could be preferentially generated on the leading strand (Pavlov et al., 2002).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on known biochemistry cited from Zheng et al., 2006; Pavlov et al., 2002.

claim: There may be differences between the efficiency of repair between the leading and lagging strand.
source: Thirdly, there may be differences between the efficiency of repair between the leading and lagging strand (Pavlov et al., 2003).
evidence: Proposed mechanism cited from Pavlov et al., 2003.

claim: The mutation pattern is consistent with the hypothesized bidirectional initiation of mtDNA genome replication.
source: Further, the mutation pattern reported here is consistent with the hypothesized bidirectional initiation of mtDNA genome replication (Yasukawa et al., 2005, 2006; Holt and Reyes, 2012).
evidence: Inferred from reversal of strand bias in D-loop and cited from Yasukawa et al., 2005, 2006; Holt and Reyes, 2012.

claim: Most of the mtDNA missense mutations become fixed in tumor progenitor cells without distinct physiological advantage.
source: It appears that most of the mtDNA missense mutations we observe become fixed in tumor progenitor cells without distinct physiological advantage.
evidence: Inferred from dN/dS analysis and VAF distributions.

claim: mtDNA somatic substitutions accumulate largely neutrally.
source: All the statistical testing performed in this study—variant allele fraction comparison across different categories of somatic mutations, number of recurrent mutations, and dN/dS ratio—suggest that mtDNA somatic substitutions accumulate largely neutrally.
evidence: Inferred from multiple statistical analyses.

claim: Of the thousands of somatic mutations found in a cancer genome, many fewer than a hundred are believed to confer a selective advantage to the cancer cell.
source: This is not different from previous observations in nuclear genomes: of the thousands of somatic mutations found in a cancer genome, many fewer than a hundred are believed to confer a selective advantage to the cancer cell (Stratton et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Stratton et al., 2009.

claim: Protein-truncating mutations occur at an appreciable rate.
source: The implication of this is that the inactivating mutations occur at an appreciable rate, but the fraction of mitochondrial genomes per cell carrying these variants cannot increase beyond a certain limit without impairing the selective fitness of that cell.
evidence: Inferred from dNonsense/dS ratio being close to 1.

claim: The fraction of mitochondrial genomes per cell carrying protein-truncating variants cannot increase beyond a certain limit without impairing the selective fitness of that cell.
source: The implication of this is that the inactivating mutations occur at an appreciable rate, but the fraction of mitochondrial genomes per cell carrying these variants cannot increase beyond a certain limit without impairing the selective fitness of that cell.
evidence: Inferred from lower VAFs of protein-truncating mutations.

claim: Having a sizable number of mitochondria with fully intact proteome remains critical to the fitness of a cancer cell.
source: Having a sizable number of mitochondria with fully intact proteome remains critical to the fitness of a cancer cell.
evidence: Inferred from negative selection against protein-truncating mutations.

claim: 109 somatic short insertions were identified.
source: Along with the 1907 somatic mtDNA substitutions, we identified 109 and 142 somatic short insertions and deletions, respectively, from the 1675 cancer mtDNA sequences using Varscan2 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Calculated from mutation data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 142 somatic short deletions were identified.
source: Along with the 1907 somatic mtDNA substitutions, we identified 109 and 142 somatic short insertions and deletions, respectively, from the 1675 cancer mtDNA sequences using Varscan2 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Calculated from mutation data in Supplementary file 2.
